claims.text: DoD self-reports a budget of $841.4 billion, 3.4 million personnel and 4,800 sites in over 160 countries, with Pete Hegseth as Secretary and Steve Feinberg as Deputy Secretary.

Executive Order 14347 of 5 September 2025 authorises 'Department of War' and 'Secretary of War' as secondary designations, states that 'Statutory references to the Department of Defense ... shall remain controlling until changed subsequently by the law', and directs a recommendation within 60 days on permanently renaming the Department.

10 U.S.C. 119 requires the Secretary of Defense to report annually by 1 March on special access programs, but permits a waiver under which the information and the justification for the waiver are provided 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' rather than to the full committees.

claims.source: Inference from the text of 10 U.S.C. 119
claims.text: The waiver provision of 10 U.S.C. 119 is the only lawful mechanism by which a multi-decade DoD program could be concealed from the bulk of the defense committees without a criminal violation; any legacy recovery program that has survived since the 1940s is therefore either a waived unacknowledged SAP, or it is unreported and therefore unlawful. Reasoning: the statute exhausts the lawful options, so the allegation reduces to a binary that Congress can test by demanding the waived-SAP list.

desc: The Department of Defense is the institution inside which every alleged element of a legacy recovery and reverse-engineering effort must, by law, sit: the Special Access Program enterprise, the service laboratories, the combat support agencies, and the contracting vehicles that move money to industry. It is also the institution that has produced the entire official denial record. As of 2026 the Department describes itself on its own site as having a budget of $841.4 billion, roughly 3.4 million personnel, and 4,800 sites in over 160 countries, with Pete Hegseth as Secretary and Steve Feinberg as Deputy Secretary. On 5 September 2025 President Trump signed Executive Order 14347, 'Restoring the United States Department of War', authorising 'Department of War' and 'Secretary of War' as secondary designations for use in official correspondence and non-statutory documents while expressly providing that 'Statutory references to the Department of Defense ... shall remain controlling until changed subsequently by the law'; the order directed the Secretary to recommend within 60 days the legislative actions needed to make the rename permanent. The Department's UAP posture runs through three successive offices - the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force, AOIMSG, and since July 2022 the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office - and through a press-guidance function that has issued the operative denials of Luis Elizondo's AATIP role and of David Grusch's retrieval allegations. The single most important structural fact about DoD for this board is that the Department's own SAP reporting statute, 10 U.S.C. 119, permits the Secretary to waive the reporting of any special access program to the defense committees and instead notify only the chairman and ranking member of each committee - a lawful mechanism by which a program can be run with four members of Congress notified and no one else, which is precisely the mechanism Grusch alleges was abused.

claims.text: The DoD Inspector General records that the Department's first official UAP-focused activity was PROJECT SIGN, established December 1947; that Air Force personnel investigated 243 sightings from 1947 to 1949; and that PROJECT BLUE BOOK investigated over 12,000 sightings between 1952 and 1969.

claims.source: Unclassified Summary of Report No. DODIG-2023-109, 24 January 2024, Historical Background; https://media.defense.gov/2024/Jan/25/2003381266/-1/-1/1/UNCLASSIFIED%20SUMMARY_UNIDENTIFIED%20ANOMALOUS%20PHENOMENA%20SECURE.PDF
claims.text: The same inspector general summary states that 'The DoD did not officially look at UAP again until mid-2000, when select members of Congress initiated and funded a program to study UAP, called the Advanced Aerospace Weapon Systems Applications program, under the direction of the Defense Intelligence Agency.'

claims.source: Unclassified Summary of Report No. DODIG-2023-109, 24 January 2024; https://media.defense.gov/2024/Jan/25/2003381266/-1/-1/1/UNCLASSIFIED%20SUMMARY_UNIDENTIFIED%20ANOMALOUS%20PHENOMENA%20SECURE.PDF - DEMOTED from Tier 1 (sourced to an interested party (AARO/DoD) asserting an external fact; primary record of the statement, not of the fact); needs primary replacement
claims.text: The inspector general found that the DoD has not used a coordinated approach to detect, report, collect, analyze and identify UAP, has issued no comprehensive UAP response plan, and does not formally require the Military Services or counterintelligence organisations to send UAP incident reports to AARO.

claims.source: Unclassified Summary of Report No. DODIG-2023-109, 24 January 2024, Recommendations 3, 4 and 5; https://media.defense.gov/2024/Jan/25/2003381266/-1/-1/1/UNCLASSIFIED%20SUMMARY_UNIDENTIFIED%20ANOMALOUS%20PHENOMENA%20SECURE.PDF
claims.text: The Secretary of the Navy, the Secretary of the Air Force and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff each declined to provide official comments for inclusion in the inspector general's final report on the Department's UAP actions.

claims.source: https://media.defense.gov/2022/Jul/20/2003039074/-1/-1/1/ESTABLISHMENT-OF-THE-ALL-DOMAIN-ANOMALY-RESOLUTION-OFFICE.PDF - DEMOTED from Tier 1 (sourced to an interested party (AARO/DoD) asserting an external fact; primary record of the statement, not of the fact); needs primary replacement
claims.text: The Deputy Secretary of Defense memorandum of 15 July 2022 directed that every DoD component holding UAP data, analysis, contracts or other material immediately synchronise with AARO, and made AARO the Department's authoritative office and focal point for all UAP activities.

claims.source: Public Law 118-31, sec. 1687, 22 December 2023; https://www.congress.gov/118/plaws/publ31/PLAW-118publ31.pdf; analysis at https://www.insidegovernmentcontracts.com/2024/01/implications-of-the-unidentified-anomalous-phenomena-uap-amendment-in-the-2024-national-defense-authorization-act-ndaa/
claims.text: Section 1687 of the FY2024 NDAA (Public Law 118-31) prohibits the use of authorised funds for special access or restricted access programme activities relating to UAP that have not been reported to the appropriate congressional committees, and extends the restriction to contractor Independent Research and Development related to UAP.

Luis Elizondo testified in writing that in his last government position he 'managed a Special Access Program on behalf of the White House and the National Security Council,' that 'the U.S. is in possession of UAP technologies,' and that the country is 'in the midst of a multi-decade, secretive arms race, one funded by misallocated taxpayer dollars and hidden from our elected representatives and oversight bodies.'

Elizondo further testified that 'the Pentagon's very own Public Affairs Office openly employs a professional psychological operations officer as the singular point of contact for any UAP-related inquiries from citizens and the media.'

AARO's Historical Record Report Volume I states that the scope of an Intelligence Community Controlled Access Program was expanded in 2021, without sufficient justification, to protect UAP reverse-engineering, and that the programme was later disestablished.

claims.source: AARO FY2025 Consolidated Annual Report on UAP, Section V.B; https://www.aaro.mil/Portals/136/PDFs/FY25%20UAP%20Annual%20Report/AARO_FY2025_Consolidated_Annual_Report_on_UAP.pdf
claims.text: The Joint Staff issued a classified UAP GENADMIN in February 2025; AARO's FY2025 report states the office aims to fully implement it, meaning the Department's UAP response doctrine is not public.

claims.source: AARO FY2025 Consolidated Annual Report on UAP, Section V.B, and Unclassified Summary of DODIG-2023-109; https://www.aaro.mil/Portals/136/PDFs/FY25%20UAP%20Annual%20Report/AARO_FY2025_Consolidated_Annual_Report_on_UAP.pdf
claims.text: The Military Services' counterintelligence, law enforcement and security agencies, identified by the inspector general as Army Counterintelligence, the Naval Criminal Investigative Service and the Air Force Office of Special Investigations, are the cognizant authorities responsible for responding to UAP incidents and incursions on all Department installations and ranges.

The Office of the Secretary of Defense is one of only seven organisations with a records transmittal listed in the National Archives UAP Records Collection, Record Group 615, as of the collection page's 22 May 2026 review date.

In February 2026 a War Department official stated that AARO 'is working in close coordination with the White House and across federal agencies to consolidate existing UAP records collections and facilitate the expeditious release of never-before-seen UAP information,' and Secretary Hegseth said the Department would be 'in full compliance with that executive order.'
In May 2026 MITRE, a federally funded research and development centre, moved to comply with a request from Representative Eric Burlison for UAP records and assets dating back to 1930.

dossier.denialPosture: The Department, through AARO, has denied since March 2024 that it has ever recovered, possessed or reverse-engineered non-human technology, and its annual reports state that all resolved cases are attributable to prosaic objects. It has never publicly enumerated its special access programme inventory in this area, and its response doctrine, the February 2025 Joint Staff UAP GENADMIN, remains classified. Three of its most senior officials declined to comment on the record for the inspector general's evaluation of its UAP conduct.
dossier.narrative:
The Department's UAP history is documented by its own inspector general. The first official DoD UAP activity was PROJECT SIGN, established by the Air Force Chief of Staff in December 1947. From 1947 to 1949 Air Force personnel investigated 243 reported sightings. In 1952 the Air Force Director of Intelligence initiated PROJECT BLUE BOOK, which investigated more than 12,000 sightings before its termination in 1969. Then, in the inspector general's own words, the DoD did not officially look at UAP again until mid-2000, when select members of Congress initiated and funded a programme to study UAP under the direction of the Defense Intelligence Agency. That sentence is worth pausing on. The Department's own watchdog records that the resumption of UAP work was not a Departmental decision at all. It was a congressional earmark inserted over the Department's disinterest, and when the Senate Majority Leader asked for it to be made a Special Access Program in June 2009 the Deputy Secretary of Defense declined on the advice of the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence.

That forty-year gap is the load-bearing claim of the official account and the weakest point in it. The Department asks the public to accept that between BLUE BOOK's closure in 1969 and AAWSAP's standup in 2008 it did nothing on the subject at all, in the same period in which it was operating an unacknowledged special access programme architecture whose whole purpose is that its contents cannot be inferred from budget documents or organisation charts.

Congress does not appear to accept it. Section 1683 of the FY2022 NDAA forced the creation of an office. Section 1673 of the FY2023 NDAA forced the creation of a reporting mechanism usable notwithstanding non-disclosure agreements and free from reprisal. Section 6802 of the FY2023 NDAA forced the historical report. Section 1687 of the FY2024 NDAA went further and prohibited the use of authorised funds for any special access or restricted access programme activity relating to UAP that has not been reported to the congressional committees by the Director of National Intelligence, and extended the restriction to contractor Independent Research and Development. Legislators do not write funding prohibitions against activities they believe do not exist.

The Deputy Secretary's July 2022 establishment memorandum is the Department's own consolidation instrument. It made AARO the authoritative office for all UAP and UAP-related activities, disestablished the Navy task force, and directed every DoD component holding UAP data, analysis, contracts or other material to synchronise immediately with AARO. If material and paperwork from a legacy programme existed anywhere in the Department, that memorandum is the order that would have moved it, and it moved it into an office reporting to the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security.

The inspector general's evaluation, DODIG-2023-109, is the best independent measure of the Department's conduct. Its unclassified summary, released 24 January 2024, found that the DoD had not used a coordinated approach to detect, report, collect, analyze, and identify UAP; that DoD components had largely excluded the geographic combatant commands, the organisations actually responsible for detecting and preventing threats against the United States; that components had developed varying informal processes; and that the Department had issued no comprehensive UAP response plan. The evaluation notes that the Military Services and counterintelligence organisations had sent some UAP incident reports to AARO but that the Department does not formally require them to do so. It also records that the Secretary of the Navy, the Secretary of the Air Force and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff each declined to provide official comments for the final report. That is three of the Department's most senior officials refusing to go on the record with the inspector general on this subject.

The response architecture matters as much as the analytic one. AARO's FY2025 report states that the military Services' counterintelligence, law enforcement and security agencies are the cognizant authorities responsible for responding to UAP incidents and incursions on all installations and ranges, and that AARO aims to fully implement the Joint Staff's classified UAP GENADMIN from February 2025. The doctrine governing what the United States military does when an anomalous object comes down on its property is classified, and the organisations that would execute it are Army Counterintelligence, the Naval Criminal Investigative Service and the Air Force Office of Special Investigations. Those are the same organisations that, in the concealment argument, would administer the silence.

Luis Elizondo, who told the House Oversight Committee in November 2024 that in his last government position he managed a Special Access Program on behalf of the White House and the National Security Council, testified in writing that UAP are real, that the United States is in possession of UAP technologies, and that the country is in the midst of a multi-decade secretive arms race funded by misallocated taxpayer dollars and hidden from elected representatives and oversight bodies. He testified that a small cadre within the government has created a culture of suppression and intimidation including unwarranted criminal investigations and harassment, and that the Pentagon's public affairs office employs a professional psychological operations officer as the single point of contact for UAP inquiries from citizens and the media.

The Department's posture since February 2026 has been transparency by executive channel. Secretary Hegseth committed to full compliance with a presidential disclosure directive, and a War Department official told DefenseScoop that AARO was working in close coordination with the White House to consolidate existing UAP records collections and facilitate the expeditious release of never-before-seen UAP information. The releases run through a departmental website rather than through the statutory National Archives collection, which puts the pace and the redactions back inside the Department.
openQuestions: No public accounting exists of unacknowledged special access programmes reviewed under section 1687 of the FY2024 NDAA, nor any report from the Director of National Intelligence identifying which UAP-related SAPs were reported to the congressional committees and which were not.
The February 2025 Joint Staff UAP GENADMIN is classified. What it directs commanders to do on encountering or recovering an anomalous object is unknown.

The forty-year gap the Department claims between BLUE BOOK's termination in 1969 and AAWSAP's standup in 2008 rests on the absence of a record, not on a record of absence, and has never been tested against the Department's SAP inventory for that period.

The Department has not published which components held UAP 'data, analysis, contracts, or other material' that were synchronised to AARO under the July 2022 memorandum, nor an inventory of what was transferred.
Whether the DOPSR prepublication review process has been used to suppress UAP-related disclosures by cleared personnel is undocumented on this board and is a Wave 5 target.
dossier.whatItIs: The Department of Defense, renamed the Department of War by executive action in 2025, is the cabinet department that has run every official US government UAP investigation from Project SIGN in December 1947 to AARO today. It holds the special access programme architecture, the counterintelligence organisations that respond to incursions on military installations, and the security review office that clears what its personnel may say in public. It is the institution against which the legacy programme allegation is principally made.
dossier.whyImplicated: The Department has controlled every official UAP investigation for seventy-nine years and, by its own inspector general's finding, still had no coordinated approach and no comprehensive response plan eighteen months after Congress ordered it to build one. Its structure gives it the two things a concealed recovery programme requires: an unacknowledged special access programme system whose existence need not be disclosed, and counterintelligence organisations designated as the first responders to any anomalous incursion on any installation or range. Congress has twice legislated as though it believes unreported UAP compartments exist, first by giving AARO statutory access notwithstanding all access controls, then by forbidding the expenditure of funds on UAP-related special access activity not reported to the intelligence committees. A former DoD official who managed a Special Access Program on behalf of the White House and the National Security Council testified under oath that the United States is in possession of UAP technologies and that the effort is hidden from elected representatives. The Department's own Historical Record Report concedes that a controlled access compartment was expanded in 2021 to protect UAP reverse-engineering.
